paraphrase: Thesis by the six marks. The sutta teaches mindfulness of breathing, in sixteen steps in four tetrads, as a practice which, developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and benefit and fulfils in turn the four establishments of mindfulness, the seven awakening factors, and knowledge and liberation (vijjāvimutti). Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): it opens with the community's advancement and the announcement of the chain (mn118:4, 15) and closes on its last link (mn118:41-43). Repetition (abhyāsa): each link is asked in the same form ('how developed, how cultivated ... fulfils'), and answered by the same formula (mn118:16, 22-23, 28-29, 40-41, 43); the awakening-factor sequence is repeated for each foundation (mn118:30-39). Novelty (apūrvatā): the sutta does not itself mark anything as new. Stated result (phala): great fruit and great benefit (mn118:15, 22), fulfilment of the four establishments, of the seven factors and of knowledge and liberation (mn118:28, 40, 43). Praise (arthavāda): the praise of the community and the list of practices its monks are engaged in (mn118:8-14) frame the teaching; the praise is of the assembly, not of the practice. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the mapping of each tetrad to a foundation is argued by the identification of the breaths as 'a body among bodies' and careful attention to the breaths as 'a feeling among feelings' (mn118:24-25), and the sequence of the seven factors is a conditioned sequence, each arising in dependence on the previous (mn118:30-36). The sutta sets out place and posture at mn118:17, and states its own condition at mn118:26: it does not speak of mindfulness of breathing for one of muddled mindfulness and without clear comprehension.
speaker: the Buddha (Bhagavā)
